name: Makhuwa-Enahara
confidence_why: Van der Wal 2009 describes Makhuwa-Enahara as a tone language without the phrase-penultimate lengthening of Makonde, Makwe or Zulu, Cheng and Kisseberth 1979-1981, Kisseberth 2003 and Kisseberth and Guérois 2014 analyse every dialect including Enahara with mora-based H tones and never mention stress, and Philippson 1991 classes Makua as a pitch accent language, so the only talk of 'stress' is Woodward 1926's remark on tense-marking prefixes in Ruvuma Makua, which the tonal accounts treat as H tones.
catalog_citation: van der Wal, Jenneke. 2009. Word order and information structure in Makhuwa-Enahara. PhD thesis, Leiden University (LOT Dissertation Series 215). Open access, hdl:1887/13845.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'A short description of Makhuwa-Enahara', §2.1.2 'Vowels' ('Long vowels') p. 20 and §2.2.2 'Intonation' p. 34; ch. 5 p. 242 and p. 245.
catalog_quote: [p. 20] The contrastiveness of length is illustrated in the minimal pairs in (33). Long vowels are written with two symbols (e.g., <aa>, not <a:>). Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde. [p. 34] 2.2.2 Intonation. Makhuwa is clearly a tonal language, but it has some intonational features as well. These include the indication of continuation of speech, question intonation, and emphasis. ... In some Bantu languages, including some with a similar conjoint/disjoint distinction such as Makonde, Makwe, Zulu and Sotho, an automatic lengthening of the penultimate syllable occurs at the end of a phonological phrase, thus indicating the right boundary of that phrase. Unlike these languages, Makhuwa does not have this penultimate lengthening. [p. 242] In English, F-marking is realised phonologically as stress, and every F-marked constituent must contain that element in the sentence with the main stress. In Makhuwa, the primary indicator of focus is not stress. [p. 245] The indication of phonological phrases by penultimate lengthening is also known for other Bantu languages and is well described for Makwe (Devos 2004), but it is not present in Makhuwa.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Makhuwa (makh1264) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Philippson 1991 (Glottolog 38907), whose Glottolog record does link Makhuwa [vmw]. The author's full-text PDF (542 pp., text) was downloaded from the DDL-CNRS site (byte-identical to the copy already), saved with a Makua-pages excerpt, the Glottolog JSON and the theses.fr record under, and logged in there. Philippson treats Makua (group XIV, P31, documentation rated '+', data second-hand from Cheng & Kisseberth 1981 and Stucky 1979, Imitthupi dialect) as a 'langue purement accentuelle' in his pitch accent sense: disyllabic stems carry the H-docking mark either on the prefix or on the stem-initial syllable (two patterns; pp. 399, 440-441, 507-508), Esaaka -cvcv stems only on the penult (fn. p. 441); his Annexe criterion 10 (status of the penultimate) records no demarcative penultimate accent for Makua, unlike Makonde-Maraba or Tumbuka/Sena. This is a tone/pitch accent statement, not word stress, and it agrees with the first-hand source already held by the project, van der Wal 2009 (pp. 20, 34: no automatic penultimate lengthening; tonal language), re-read here and given as the best statement. No source read states a word-stress position for Makhuwa. nothing remains to acquire from the item list.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Makhuwa is described as a tonal language (morphologically assigned H tones with tone doubling; lexical tone contrasts marginal per Kisseberth 2003). The only statements about stress-like prominence are negative: the language lacks the automatic phrase-penultimate lengthening typical of neighbouring Bantu languages, vowel length is lexically contrastive, and focus is not marked by stress. No source opened states a position for word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final long vowels occur only in ideophones or under emphasis; under emphasis the last syllable of a phrase 'can sometimes be lengthened' with a HL pattern (p. 34-35). Phrase-final position blocks tone doubling (Final Lowering / Long Fall).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the phonological phrase / sentence (penultimate lengthening as a phrase-boundary cue) rather than the word; van der Wal's data are Makhuwa-Enahara (Ilha de Moçambique, Nampula). Kisseberth 2003 (Ruvuma dialects) and Cheng & Kisseberth 1979-81 (Ikorovere) describe tone only.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement describes Makhuwa-Enahara, the variety of Ilha de Moçambique (Glottolog dialect 'Enaharra', enah1238, under makh1264). Kisseberth 2003 and Cheng & Kisseberth 1979-81 describe the Ruvuma dialects Ikorovere and Imitthupi of southern Tanzania (Glottolog may file these under Makhuwa-Meetto rather than makh1264); Sacramento 1906 is coastal Mozambican 'macúa' of unspecified dialect. All sources agree Makhuwa is tonal.

new_statements.quote: In some Bantu languages, including some with a similar conjoint/disjoint distinction such as Makonde, Makwe, Zulu and Sotho, an automatic lengthening of the penultimate syllable occurs at the end of a phonological phrase, thus indicating the right boundary of that phrase. new_statements.citation: van der Wal, Jenneke. 2009. Word order and information structure in Makhuwa-Enahara. PhD thesis, Leiden University (LOT 215).
new_statements.reading: Makhuwa has no word-level stress statement in the first-hand literature: it is a tone language (mora-based H tones) with no automatic penultimate lengthening, i.e. no demarcative penultimate stress of the kind found in Makonde, Makwe, Zulu or Sotho. Philippson 1991 (the only works with stress in the title; second-hand, Imitthupi dialect) corroborates from the tonological side: Makua is a 'langue purement accentuelle' in his pitch accent sense (H docks on prefix or stem-initial; two patterns), and his Annexe criterion 10 (status of the penultimate) lists no demarcative penultimate accent for Makua (pp. 399, 440-441, 507-508). If the language is ever added to the catalog, the classification would be 'no word stress / tone (pitch accent)'; no source read gives a fixed stress position.

new_statements.quote: In all of Emakhuwa, verb stems have no lexical tone contrast. While a stem may lack any High, as in the negative infinitive, in most tenses an H is assigned to one or two moras in the stem. These stem H tones are what this volume refers to as "melodic" H tones. [...] In all dialects the tonal contrast is presence of H on a mora versus its absence. Throughout this paper, surface H is marked by an acute accent. Toneless moras are unmarked. [p. 187:] The S3 H tone corresponds to a Penult H tone in a few dialects (Imitthupi in Tanzania, Enahara in Nampula, and "Zanzibari", the language of the descendants of freed slaves who were brought to Durban in the nineteenth century).
new_statements.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. & Rozenn Guérois. 2014. Melodic H tones in Emakhuwa and Ecuwabo verbs. Africana Linguistica 20: 181-205.
new_statements.locator: p. 182, §2 'Emakhuwa' (also p. 187, §2.3 on the S3/Penult melodic H, which names Enahara)

Read…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statements (van der Wal 2009, Philippson 1991): Makhuwa is a mora-based H-tone language and nothing is said about word stress. Adds that the Enahara dialect specifically realises the S3 melodic H as a penult H tone (a tone rule, not stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Purely tonal description: the only contrast is H on a mora vs. its absence; verb stems carry grammatical (melodic) H tones assigned to macrostem mora 1, mora 2, stem mora 3 or (in Enahara, Imitthupi, Zanzibari) the penult mora, with dialect-specific H doubling and attenuation. The word 'stress' does not occur in the article; 'accent' appears only as the acute-accent notation for H; 'penult' only as phrase-penult mora in tone rules. No statement on word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Kisseberth & Guérois 2014 covers eight Emakhuwa dialects and names Enahara (Nampula) explicitly as one where the S3 melodic H is realised on the penult mora. Woodward 1926 describes the Makua of the Ruvuma district (southern Tanganyika, UMCA Masasi area; revision of Maples 1879), i.e. the 'Rovuma' dialects (Imeetto/Ikorovere/Imitthupi), not Enahara. Katupha 1983 (unopened) is on the Esaaka dialect. Salt 1814's 'Makooa' wordlist was collected at Mosambique in 1809 (Enahara/Nampula coast).

tone_statements.citation: Ngunga, Armindo & Carlos J. Manuel. 2025. Emakhuwa (P31). In The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages, 981-996. Oxford: Oxford University Press. doi:10.1093/oso/9780198808343.003.0079.
tone_statements.quote: Most variants of Makhuwa (including Enahara) are tonal and can be analysed as having a H(igh) and a L(ow) tone. Nouns and verbs have one or two underlying H tones. The position of the H tones is partly determined lexically (nouns) and partly by the grammatical form (nouns, verbs). An important property of the tonal system of Makhuwa is that H tones come in pairs; that is, the underlying H tones are doubled (Stucky 1979, Katupha 1983). ... The first H doubles onto the next tone bearing element, which is the nasal [m]
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones (H, L). Nouns and verbs have one or two underlying H tones, placed lexically or grammatically, each doubled onto the next tone-bearing element (incl. syllabic nasals). Predicative Lowering deletes the first H of predicative and post-conjoint focused nouns; final H boundary tone.

tone_statements.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2022. Attenuated High Tones in Emakhuwa Dialectology. Radical: A Journal of Phonology 4: 595-645. (reviewers: Cedric Patin, Michael Becker; posted 19 October 2022)
tone_statements.quote: The cornerstone of Makua tonology is a principle that we refer to as High Tone Doubling (HTD) . This rule simply says that a high tone associated with one tone-bearing unit is also manifested on the immediately following tone-bearing unit. ... the data in (1) show that the tone-bearing unit in Makua is the vowel rather than the syllable. ... In Makua, every noun has (at the lexical level) at least one primary high tone. Some nouns have two or more primary high tones. ... There are no lexical tone contrasts in Makua verbal stems.
tone_statements.locator: p. 124 (HTD), p. 125 (tone-bearing unit = vowel), p. 126 (nouns), p. 138-139 concluding section (verb stems)
tone_statements.summary: High vs low (no explicit toneme count); Imithupi mid and falling tones are rule-derived (Mid-Tone, Short Fall). TBU = vowel/mora plus some pre-consonantal nasals, lexically marked. Nouns carry lexical primary H; verb stems toneless, H by construction. No stress info.

tone_statements.quote: Some Emakhuwa (Bantu, P30) dialects exhibit a phenomenon of High Tone Doubling, where underlying (or “primary”) H tones double onto the immediately following mora. Some of these dialects attenuate or weaken the primary H tone, once it has doubled, under certain conditions. This attenuation may be partial or complete.
tone_statements.locator: Abstract, journal landing page (radical.cnrs.fr); article pp. 595-645

tone_statements.summary: Privative H vs toneless moras; underlying (primary) H doubles onto the next mora; in some dialects the primary H is then partially or fully attenuated (lowered) under stated conditions.

tone_statements.summary: Tone present and characterised as grammatical (no lexical tone contrast), per the chapter abstract.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement, because no source gives a word-stress position. The one terminological tension is Woodward 1926 (Ruvuma Makua), who twice speaks of a 'stress' that distinguishes verb tenses (on the third-singular prefix aa- of the past tense, on the first syllable of the Past Conditional kátunale), whereas Kisseberth & Guérois 2014, van der Wal 2009 and Philippson 1991 describe the same prefix prominences as H tones in a purely tonal system. Read in that light Woodward's remarks are compatible with the tonal reading and give no fixed stress position. Salt 1814 is silent; the two Katupha theses could not be opened.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2022. Attenuated High Tones in Emakhuwa Dialectology. Radical: A Journal of Phonology 4: 595-645. (reviewers: Cedric Patin, Michael Becker; posted 19 October 2022)
sources.quote: The cornerstone of Makua tonology is a principle that we refer to as High Tone Doubling (HTD) . This rule simply says that a high tone associated with one tone-bearing unit is also manifested on the immediately following tone-bearing unit. ... the data in (1) show that the tone-bearing unit in Makua is the vowel rather than the syllable. ... In Makua, every noun has (at the lexical level) at least one primary high tone. Some nouns have two or more primary high tones. ... There are no lexical tone contrasts in Makua verbal stems.
sources.locator: p. 124 (HTD), p. 125 (tone-bearing unit = vowel), p. 126 (nouns), p. 138-139 concluding section (verb stems)
sources.note: High vs low (no explicit toneme count); Imithupi mid and falling tones are rule-derived (Mid-Tone, Short Fall). TBU = vowel/mora plus some pre-consonantal nasals, lexically marked. Nouns carry lexical primary H; verb stems toneless, H by construction. No stress info.

sources.quote: Some Emakhuwa (Bantu, P30) dialects exhibit a phenomenon of High Tone Doubling, where underlying (or “primary”) H tones double onto the immediately following mora. Some of these dialects attenuate or weaken the primary H tone, once it has doubled, under certain conditions. This attenuation may be partial or complete.

sources.note: 'Some Emakhuwa (Bantu, P30) dialects exhibit a phenomenon of High Tone Doubling, where underlying (or "primary") H tones double onto the immediately following mora. Some of these dialects attenuate or weaken the primary H tone, once it has doubled, under certain conditions. This attenuation may be partial or complete. The present paper describes in detail the conditions under which attenuation occurs in these dialects.. The conclusion is that attenuation is phonological in nature.' tone.quote: Bernardo (2009a) refere também que em algumas variantes de Emakhuwa, como Exirima, por exemplo, se verifica ainda o contraste de significados de palavras através do tom. Mas para o nosso estudo, este suprassegmento não será levado muito em consideração, muito menos será representado nos dados analisados, uma vez que a variante em estudo apresenta poucas marcas tonais, encontradas especificamente em nomes, para além de que o sistema de ortografia vigente da línga em análise ainda não tem a sua representação padronizada.
tone.locator: p. 24, ch. III sec. 3.1.1 'Aspectos preliminares da fonologia de Emakhuwa', closing paragraph on syllable and tone
tone.translation: Bernardo (2009a) also notes that in some variants of Emakhuwa, such as Exirima, word meanings are also contrasted by tone. But for our study this suprasegment will not be given much consideration, still less represented in the data analysed, since the variant under study shows few tonal marks, found specifically in nouns, and moreover the current orthography of the language under analysis does not yet have a standardized representation of it.
tone.summary: MA thesis on recent-past verb allomorphy in Nampula Emakhuwa; tone set aside in one sentence: the variety has 'few tonal marks, only in nouns' (ambiguous between contrasts and written marks), none transcribed; tonal contrasts in Exirima credited to Bernardo 2009a. No inventory, nothing on stress.
